title: The world, close
hook: the Zen ox-herding pictures don't end on the mountain or in the empty circle: the herder walks back into the market with helping hands
tomorrow: one arrow hits. where does the second one come from?

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: quiet good. Amar Das carried the water in the dark. Two weeks out in the world now: the poor, the earth, neighbors, strangers, creatures, speech, money, peace, conscience. Today, the last picture.
screen: `QUIET GOOD.` → `TWO WEEKS IN THE WORLD.` → `THE LAST PICTURE.`

segments.voice: A crowded hallway, a loud group chat, a tense meeting. Some days the dream is a cabin far from all of it. Zen has a set of pictures about that dream: the ten ox-herding pictures. A herder has lost his ox, which Zen teachers read as his own true nature. He follows the tracks. He glimpses it, catches it, tames it, and rides it home playing a flute. Then the ox is gone, then the herder too: an empty circle. That sounds like the end.
screen: `A DREAM OF A CABIN.` → `THE TEN OX-HERDING PICTURES.` → `CAUGHT, TAMED, RIDDEN HOME.` → `AN EMPTY CIRCLE.`

segments.voice: It isn't. After the empty circle comes a picture of the plain world: the river flowing on, the flowers simply red. And then the last picture. The herder walks into town. Barefoot, chest bare, a gourd at his side, mixing with people in the market. The title says he enters the city with bliss-bestowing hands. The verse beside it says that, without any magic powers, he makes withered trees bloom. That's the Zen teaching the series lands on: awakening isn't finished on the mountain or in the silence. It's finished in the marketplace, among ordinary people, helping. In the pictures, practice doesn't lift the herder out of the world. It brings him back into it, lighter, with open hands. Not preaching at anyone. Just there, and useful. And notice who he is by then: nobody special to look at. A cheerful man in the crowd, the kind of neighbor whose name you learn.
screen: `THE RIVER FLOWS, THE FLOWERS ARE RED.` · `BAREFOOT INTO THE MARKET.` · `BLISS-BESTOWING HANDS.` · `NOBODY SPECIAL, JUST USEFUL.` · then, large: `IN THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: Take a pen and write down one change from these two weeks in the world: a name you learned, a reply you didn't send, a share you gave. One line is enough. Then rest your hands open on your knees, the way the herder walks into town, until the sit is done.
The world: in Zen's last ox-herding picture, the marketplace, where the herder comes back with open, helping hands.
Pocket this one: in the world, back in the market with open hands. That closes two weeks out here; see you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1734 COUNTS.` → `IN THE WORLD · 14 OF 14.` → `TOMORROW: ONE ARROW HITS. WHERE DOES THE SECOND ONE COME FROM?`

howItsDone: Zen teachers use the ten ox-herding pictures, with their short verses, to describe the stages of practice. The last picture, returning to the marketplace, is read as practice lived among ordinary people.

Zen.meaning: a school of Buddhism centered on meditation

ox-herding pictures.meaning: a Zen series of ten images and verses about the path

gourd.meaning: a dried, hollow fruit shell used as a bottle

bliss-bestowing hands.meaning: the tenth picture's phrase: hands that bring others joy

sources.ref: The Ten Ox-Herding Pictures, with verses attributed to Kuoan Shiyuan (the search, the tracks, seeing, catching, taming, riding home, the ox forgotten, the empty circle, returning to the source, entering the city with bliss-bestowing hands)

notes: 2026-10-15 v3: written new in recipe v3, shape life; closes the 'In the world' stretch (days 1721-1734). Story: the ten ox-herding pictures. Teaching named: in Zen the path ends in the marketplace with helping hands, not on the mountain. Hook answers day 1733's question. Cold Mountain (day 1550) also touched the mountain theme; this day turns the other way.

Check: the ox 'read as true nature' is labeled a reading. The tenth picture's details (barefoot, chest bare, a gourd or wine bottle, withered trees blooming without magic powers) follow the usual translations of Kuoan's verse and comment, paraphrased; other series (e.g. with eight or six pictures) differ. 'The ten ox-herding pictures' is the series' name, not a counted claim.
